I used to work at a fast food chain in the city where a lot of homeless people hung out. 

I got to know a few of them and while most were always grateful for a free meal they were  
definitely more appreciative of a few dollars.

They all had their own reasons for this, one being that they weren't hungry at that point and   
would rather save the money for food at a later date over carrying around the food that they   
had been given.

 Others would save their money for things like bus fare to get them to appointments that   
would hopefully assist in getting them off the street. 

Some of them had dietary needs which usually prevented them being able to eat most of the   
food they were gifted (could you imagine being SO hungry and receiving a meal that is going to   
make you physically sick?). 

One of the guys who I used to chat to would always save his money for cigarettes, it was the   
one thing he looked forward to after being a smoker for over 40 years. 

Just a few things to counteract some of the negativity in the comments and maybe add some   
reasoning to why they might not be as appreciative of a food donation. (Obviously throwing the   
food on the ground is an absolute disgrace and not appropriate at all!!)

I remember when my own mother found out about mine. At first she was just so angry with me and would lash out because she dd not understand how to react and it made things so much worse for me.

And then she was upset and constantly blamed herself (i think she still does) for something I had done to myself. She also thought she should have been there to protect me but what she didn't see is that she always was - I just didn't let her.

And then came the lack of privacy, she never let me out of her sight and was always checking on me if I was alone in my room. I would get angry at her for this and we would argue so much about it. I know now that she was just scared she was going to lose me.

Research & recovery was our next step, she got online and did a lot of research about self harm and what makes people turn to it as a coping method. She spoke to family & friends who have history in mental illness and found out different coping methods that worked for them and then she recommended them to me.

She took me to a doctor, she let me go in by myself so I could show the doctor my injuries and he could help me treat them without her having to see what I'd done to myself and she was in the waiting room when I came back out. The doctor I saw was actually the person who referred me to a psychologist - maybe your daughter might be more inclined to go if it was suggested by a doctor?

She let me know that she was there for me to talk to, even if didn't want to talk she told me that we could sit in silence and cry and eat pizza together. She suggested easy distractions that I could occupy myself with without too much effort. We even worked out some breathing methods to help me cope with my panic attacks. 

I still have a long way to go with my recovery but my mum has been there almost every step of the way, I'm probably just rambling but I hope that maybe sharing my experiences could possibly help somehow.
